## The Museum of Almost

The Museum of Almost stood between a shop that mended umbrellas and a shop that sold them, an arrangement visitors found amusing until they came out again.

Its caretaker, Mr. Iven, had worked there for thirty-eight years. He was a narrow, patient man with a talent for hearing dust settle. Each morning he unlocked the six galleries and went among the exhibits with a yellow duster.

There was the ticket to Trieste, never punched. There was the wedding ring that had spent forty years in a waistcoat pocket, waiting for a question its owner had been too happy to ask. In Gallery Three, a telephone rang once every eleven minutes; no one had ever answered it. Gallery Five held only a kitchen chair, facing a window through which it was always the first snow of winter.

The labels were small and deliberately unhelpful. NEARLY, 1962. THE WRONG KIND OF COURAGE. A LIFE, ADEQUATELY IMAGINED.

Visitors were asked not to spend more than ten minutes with any one exhibit. This was not because the exhibits were dangerous, Mr. Iven explained, but because people tended to mistake recognition for instruction.

Nothing had been bought. Objects arrived in the post, or were left on the step, or simply appeared overnight with their labels already typed. Once, an entire apple orchard had been delivered in a cigar box. Mr. Iven kept it in his desk and, on difficult afternoons, opened the lid a fraction to let out the smell of October.

His own life, he sometimes thought, would have made a poor exhibit. It had been too consistent to be interesting. He had nearly done a great number of things, but nearly doing them had required so much daily attention that the years had filled up.

On the last Tuesday in October, just as he was thinking of closing, a woman came in with rain on her shoulders. He knew her at once, though he had imagined the meeting so often that the real woman, with water on her eyelashes and a loose thread at her cuff, seemed like an imperfect reconstruction.

“Mara,” he said.

“You look old.”

“Yes.”

“I meant it kindly.”

“Then thank you.”

They had not seen each other since their mother’s funeral, when they had divided the furniture with such ferocious courtesy that there had been nothing left to say.

Mara set a small rectangle of card on the counter. On one side was the name of a hotel that had burned down years ago. On the other, in pencil, was his address. Beneath it she had written: ALMOST KNOCKED.

“Your flat,” she said. “Twelve years ago. I was at that hotel for a conference. I stood outside your building for twenty minutes.”

“I was probably here.”

“You were always here.”

This was not quite cruel, which made it worse.

She had found the card in a book, she said. She was clearing out. Or clearing up; she could never remember which was which. It had seemed wasteful to throw it away.

“I thought you might want it for the museum.”

In Gallery Three, the telephone rang. Mr. Iven waited until it stopped.

“We can’t accept it,” he said.

“Because it might still happen?”

“Because you’re here.”

“That doesn’t count. I nearly didn’t come.”

He looked at her then, properly. There was a pale scar at her eyebrow that he did not remember. He felt a brief, unreasonable anger at everything that had gone on without his permission.

Mara glanced toward Gallery Five, where the snow was falling with admirable persistence.

“Do you get used to it?” she asked.

“To what?”

“All this practice at being unhappy.”

He had never thought of it that way. The museum had always seemed to him a place where things were spared the vulgarity of endings.

She picked up the card. For one terrible second he saw how easily the next few minutes would go: her apology, his reassurance, the door closing, the rain continuing with no particular ill will. Another exhibit, adequately imagined.

“Are you hungry?” he asked.

She stared at him. “That’s a very sudden question.”

“I’m sixty-four. I can be sudden if I like.”

She laughed once, unwillingly.

“I could eat,” she said.

For the first time in thirty-eight years, Mr. Iven closed early. He changed the sign, took his coat from its peg, and left the yellow duster on the counter like a small, retired animal.

Outside, Mara opened her umbrella. After some awkward geometry, they arranged themselves beneath it. Behind them, in the blue dusk of the galleries, all the almosts kept their appointments with nothing. The telephone rang. The snow began. The ticket to Trieste remained, with exquisite patience, unpunched.

At the corner, she took his arm. They did not discuss the past. The past had six rooms and a yellow duster; it could manage without him for one evening.
